text: Last lesson built an Azure resource group and VNet. This lesson builds the real AWS equivalent — the same two-subnet network, the same CIDR blocks, but with the real aws provider and a resource schema that differs from azurerm's in some genuinely useful ways worth noticing side by side.

Declaring aws in required_providers looks just like declaring azurerm did in Lesson 1 — a source and a version constraint. The provider block underneath is different, though: azurerm needed an empty features {} block, while aws needs a region, because AWS has no single global endpoint — every API call the provider makes is scoped to one region.

aws_vpc takes one required argument, cidr_block, set here to the same 10.0.0.0/16 Lesson 5 gave its VNet. Notice there's no name argument at all — AWS's convention is a Name key inside the generic tags map instead, which is what actually shows up as the resource's label in the console, not a dedicated schema field the way azurerm's name was.

Each aws_subnet sets vpc_id, cidr_block, and availability_zone — that last one pinning the subnet to exactly one AZ, the same rule the AWS Networking course's CLI examples already covered. us-east-1a for the web subnet, us-east-1b for the app subnet, so a single AZ failing doesn't take both down.

Compare vpc_id = aws_vpc.example.id to Lesson 5's virtual_network_name = azurerm_virtual_network.example.name. azurerm_subnet referenced its VNet by a plain name string you chose yourself. aws_subnet references its VPC by a generated id — something like vpc-0abc123456789def0 — that Terraform reads back out of state automatically. Same implicit-dependency mechanics underneath, a different kind of value flowing through the reference.

Next lesson provisions real compute into both of these networks — an Azure VM into Lesson 5's subnets and an AWS instance into this lesson's subnets — and that's where azurerm and aws diverge again, this time over whether a VM even needs a separate network interface resource at all.
